prompt.1: A new Surrey hospital is under construction, and schools are crowded. What should the province do first?
prompt.2: Surrey's new hospital opens in 2030, its emergency room is busy and schools keep growing. What should the province focus on?
prompt.3: How should the province handle Surrey's new hospital under construction, its busy emergency room and its crowded schools?
prompt.4: How should the province handle Surrey's hospital, emergency room and school space as the city grows?
prompt.5: The Cloverdale hospital (about $2.88 billion) opens in 2030, 8.4% of Surrey Memorial emergency patients left without being seen in 2024, and the school district expects 700 to 800 more students a year. Choose the approach.

context.1: A new hospital is being built in Cloverdale, but it will not open until 2030. More patients now leave the busy Surrey Memorial emergency room before a doctor sees them. Many students learn in portable classrooms. Parties disagree on how to pay for more.
context.2: The province pays to build hospitals and schools. The new Cloverdale hospital will open in 2030, three years later than first planned. At Surrey Memorial, more emergency patients now leave before being seen. Surrey schools had 361 portables in 2023. The province is borrowing heavily, and parties disagree on how fast to build and how to pay.
context.3: The NDP government is building the Cloverdale hospital and new school seats, and promises 20 clinics and faster licensing for doctors trained abroad. The Conservatives say they are 'contemplating' the hospital and offer emergency room funding and a wait-time commission. The Greens want a health centre in every riding. CentreBC would build a new tower at Surrey Memorial, plan a children's hospital and add 25,000 school seats across BC. OneBC would allow private clinics.
context.4: The Cloverdale hospital's cost rose from $1.72 billion to about $2.88 billion, and its opening slipped from 2027 to 2030. In 2024, Surrey Memorial's emergency doctors said 8.4% of patients leave without being seen. The Surrey school district has asked for $5.49 billion and had 361 portables in 2023. In 2016 the NDP promised to remove all of Surrey's portables within four years of taking office, and that pledge was not met.
context.5: The Cloverdale hospital was half built in March 2026, with completion in August 2029, patients in 2030 and a cost of about $2.88 billion, up from $1.72 billion. In a September 2024 letter, Surrey Memorial emergency doctors said 8.4% of patients leave without being seen, up from 2.9% in 2020-21. Surrey enrolment passed 83,000 in 2024-25; the district expects 700 to 800 more students a year and about 87,000 by 2035, has asked for $5.49 billion for 76 projects, and had 361 portables in 2023. About 2,300 seats were under construction in August 2025; an 800-seat addition at Fleetwood Park Secondary is in design, with building due to start in winter 2027. Budget 2026 set provincial capital spending at $18.7 billion, below the $20.4 billion forecast.

text.1: Keep building the hospital and schools, add clinics, and borrow and tax top earners.
text.2: Finish the hospital and classrooms, add clinics, fast-track doctors trained abroad, and borrow and tax top earners.
text.3: Build the hospital, school seats and clinics, fast-track doctors trained abroad, and pay through borrowing plus a tax on top earners.
text.4: Keep building the hospital for 2030 and new school seats, add 20 clinics, help foreign-trained doctors qualify, and expand diagnostics, funded by deficits and a new top tax bracket.
text.5: Build the Cloverdale hospital and schools within the $18.7 billion capital plan, add 20 clinics, 1,000 training seats and diagnostics, and fund it with deficits and top tax rates of 18.8%, 22.5% and 24.5%.

text.2: Fund emergency rooms, let seniors choose their care home, focus schools on basics, and raise no taxes.
text.3: Fund emergency rooms, set up a wait-time commission, let care funding follow the senior, and focus schools on basics.
text.4: Add no new taxes, fund emergency rooms, run a 100-day wait-time commission, review care-home design rules, let funding follow seniors to non-government providers, and focus schools on basics.
text.5: Create a $50 million emergency fund and a 100-day commission, review long-term care design rules, let care funding follow the senior, make no health cuts, and raise no new taxes.

text.1: Open a local health centre, feed every student, and tax the richest to pay.
text.2: Open a Fleetwood health centre, fully fund help for students with extra needs, feed every student, and tax the richest.
text.3: Open a Fleetwood health centre, fully fund inclusive education for students with extra needs, provide school food and counsellors, and add a wealth tax.
text.4: Put a community health centre in every riding, close the inclusive education funding gap, fund a counsellor per 250 students and food for every student, and add a wealth tax.
text.5: Open an integrated health centre in every riding, fully fund inclusive education, fund a counsellor per 250 students, school food and supplies, and a wage grid for early childhood educators, with a wealth tax.

text.1: Build a new Surrey Memorial tower and a children's hospital, and add classrooms.
text.2: Build a Surrey Memorial tower, plan a children's hospital, add school seats, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.
text.3: Build a Surrey Memorial tower, plan a children's hospital, add 25,000 school seats, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.

text.1: Let private clinics open beside public hospitals, and test students more at school.
text.2: Let private clinics open alongside public hospitals to shorten waits, and add province-wide school tests.
text.3: Allow private clinics beside public hospitals to cut waits, and bring in standardized school testing.
text.4: Allow private clinics alongside public care to relieve Surrey hospitals, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, and bring in standardized testing.
text.5: Allow private clinics alongside public care to relieve Surrey hospitals, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, and bring in standardized testing in schools.

text.1: This party is building the new hospital and new classrooms, and wants more clinics.
text.3: The NDP is building the Cloverdale hospital and new Surrey school seats, and promises 20 clinics and faster licensing for doctors trained abroad. The hospital's cost rose about $1 billion and its opening slipped three years. It did not meet its 2016 promise to end Surrey's portables within four years.
text.5: The Cloverdale hospital now costs about $2.88 billion, up from $1.72 billion, with completion in August 2029 instead of 2027. The NDP is building a medical school at Simon Fraser University in Surrey and 60 mental health beds in Surrey, including involuntary care, due in spring 2028. About 2,300 school seats are under construction and 19 of 40 modular buildings replaced portables, but the district had a $16 million budget shortfall in 2025-26. For 2026 it promises 20 clinics, help for foreign-trained doctors, 1,000 training seats, and eight MRI machines and 10 CT scanners across BC. Candidate Brar promises 'a new hospital' with no timeline.

text.1: This party wants to keep emergency rooms open and is still deciding about the new hospital.
text.3: Asked about the hospital on October 7, Doerkson said 'we're contemplating all of that for our platform rollout'. Its health plan offers emergency room funding, a 100-day wait-time commission, no cuts, and long-term care funding that follows the senior. It has no Surrey school pledge.
text.5: Asked about the hospital on October 7, Doerkson said 'we're contemplating all of that for our platform rollout'. Its Keep Emergency Rooms Open plan (October 5) offers a $50 million emergency fund, a 100-day expert commission and a promise to keep current health care spending in place; on October 12 the party restated that care would stay universal and publicly funded. Its seniors plan (October 9) reviews long-term care design rules, lets care funding follow the senior and offers a choice of home care provider. It has no position on school capital or Surrey Memorial. Candidate Purewal has published only party themes.

text.1: This party would build a hospital tower and a children's hospital, add classrooms, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.
text.3: CentreBC's October 10 platform builds the Surrey Memorial acute-care tower with a published budget, starting by 2030 and opening about 2035. It plans a Surrey-Langley children's hospital, adds 25,000 school seats by 2031 and promises everyone a regular doctor or nurse. It pays through attrition and administrative cuts, not new taxes, and does not mention the Cloverdale hospital.
text.5: The platform builds the Surrey Memorial tower announced in 2024, with new operating rooms and cardiac intensive care. It completes the business case, site and design for a children's hospital south of the Fraser in its first term, with construction in 2031. It adds 25,000 school seats by 2031 with $750 million and promises primary care for all by 2031 with 600 nurse practitioners. It would have 2,500 long-term care beds under construction and 1,000 open by March 2031, and plans $3.2 billion in health capital over four years. It does not name the Cloverdale hospital or Surrey's school district.

scoring_rationale: Applies the provincial health and education positions to Surrey's two biggest capital files. a = NDP (4), with the cost overrun and portable pledge noted in the explainer; CentreBC 2 (the same builds, clinics and foreign-doctor pipeline, but it rejects the borrowing and top-earner tax in the option and funds them by attrition); Green 2 (would continue the builds but fund them differently); Conservative 1 ('contemplating'); OneBC 0. b = Conservative (4); CentreBC 2 (ER law and fund, LTC beds, letter grades and no new taxes, but rejects portable funding to non-government providers, the option's defining element, as in the provincial health question); OneBC 2 (private-pay direction, no position on the ER fund, portable funding or school basics beyond testing); NDP 1. c = Green (4); NDP 2; CentreBC 2 (counsellors 1:400, 1,500 EAs and school food to 40%, but no health centre per riding or wealth tax). d = CentreBC's platform (4): SMH tower, children's hospital, 25,000 seats, primary-care teams, LTC; NDP 2 (it announced the SMH tower in 2024 and builds seats and LTC; a symmetry fix from 1 after the option was rewritten; no children's hospital or published-budget commitment); Conservative 2 (LTC first, no new taxes, hospital undecided); Green 1; OneBC 1. e = OneBC (4); Conservative 1 (dropped 2024 private-clinic plank). Safety and SOGI content belong to their own questions and are not repeated here. Candidates inherit party scores; honesty note: none has published a position that differs from their party on either file.
